PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AID ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING A LEVEL OF GNP
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to establish a level of 0.7 per cent of the Gross National Product for official developmental aid.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to bring this motion before the House. I am very thankful that the committee, in its wisdom, decided that this would be one of the motions which could be voted upon.
The purpose of my motion is to send a strong signal to the Government that it should establish the level of official development assistance at .7 per cent of the Gross National Product, and that this should be established by legislation rather than simply at the whim of the Government of the day. It is important for all Hon. Members to be able to vote on it, and I hope the process will continue so that the issue can come to a vote.
June 17, 1986

Official Developmental Aid
I want to see this level established by law in order to remove it from the vagaries and uncertainties of the budgetary process. The development needs of the world are too great for them to be subjected to the different political and financial priorities of our Governments. When we change Government, we naturally change priorities. Canadians, and the world in general, must recognize that this is a fundamental priority which should not be subjected to that kind of whim or change. It should not be possible to change our goals in this respect without the matter even coming before Parliament in the form of a Bill.
Parliament already recognizes that there are certain areas which need this kind of protection. We have legislation establishing formulae for such things as family allowances, old age security, established programs funding, and equalization payments. As a matter of fact, the Government just finished announcing closure on a Bill to change the formula for Established Programs Financing. We do not like to see some of the changes of the Government, but at least it must come before Parliament when it wants to make a change. That important principle should also be incorporated into our entire foreign aid program.
The need for such a principle in our foreign aid program or development assistance program can be seen by looking at the history of the way in which we have dealt with the entire .7 per cent program. The .7 per cent of the Gross National Product goal for official development assistance was first accepted by the Canadian Government in 1970, following the recommendation in the Pearson report which was done for the United Nations. That report recommended that each aid giver should increase commitments of official development assistance to the level necessary for net disbursements, to reach .7 per cent of the GNP by 1975 or shortly thereafter. It also indicated that in no case should it be later than 1980. It is worth repeating that the report recommended 1975 as the target date and that it should be no later than 1980. We accepted this somewhat like a reluctant bridegroom in 1970, but we did not set any timetable for it. In 1980, we said we would make our best effort to reach the .7 per cent goal by 1990. That promise was repeated in 1983 by the Liberal Government. In the 1984 election campaign, the goal was endorsed by all three political Parties.
At that time the Canadian Council for International Cooperation asked candidates of all three Parties in 135 different ridings whether they supported increased, untied development assistance. The background material sent out by the Council explained the .7 per cent target. It is very instructive to look at the results of the survey, in that 91 per cent of the candidates who responded were elected to the House of Commons in the 1984 election. Of the 91 elected, 63 were Conservatives, 12 were Liberals and 16 were New Democrats. Of this total from all three Parties, 81 said that they supported increased aid; 81 out of 91 respondents supported increased aid, five were negative, and five were uncertain. This indicates a very high
level of political support for the principle of increased aid or increased developmental assistance.
When the new Government was sworn into office in September, 1984, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) went to New York and appeared before the 39th General Assembly of the United Nations. At that time he made a very good speech, from which I should like to quote. He said:
Our new Government intends to maintain Canada's commitment to reaching .7 per cent of the GNP by 1990 in Official Development Assistance.
That was the commitment which the Secretary of State for External Affairs made on behalf of Canadians to the people of the world at the United Nations in September, 1984. That was after the new Government was elected and all its promises were shiny and bright; some people thought that the Government might even keep them.
Then came November and the financial statement introduced by the Government in which the .7 per cent goal for ODA was postponed from 1990 to 1995. Further, in the February Budget of this year, it was postponed to the 21st century. The budget speech indicated that in the Government's perception the economy had performed better than expected. It said that the economy was doing well. Despite that, it cut back on the timetable for reaching the goal of .7 per cent of GNP for official development assistance.
Also the Secretary of State said:
Despite serious economic problems at home, we shall not turn our backs on the world's disadvantaged peoples.
In 1986 the Government said that the economy had improved better than expected, but it turned its back and postponed the goal once again.
In the past year Canadian attitudes toward development assistance and aid generally have been documented by Decima Research in a project commissioned by the Canadian Emergency Co-ordinator for African Aid. The results were made available in a little booklet entitled "How Much Aid?", which I urge all Hon. Members to read. It is available from CIDA. Some of the more interesting conclusions in the survey show that a growing percentage of young people want Canada to become a world leader in providing aid rather than being eleventh out of 21 OECD countries.
Young people particularly do not want Canada to be a mediocre follower. They want to see Canada as a leader which takes seriously the problems of world hunger and world underdevelopment. Despite a general desire to restrain Government spending, the survey indicated that 74 per cent of Canadians opposed cutting back on foreign aid. That is exactly what was done when the Government postponed the timetable for increasing aid to the .7 per cent goal.
Also Decima found that 39 per cent of the people interviewed thought that poverty .and hunger were the most serious issues facing the world. This was compared with 24 per cent who named the arms race and 22 per cent who named economic problems. A majority of people, whatever they chose
June 17, 1986

as the main problem facing the world, did not see the Government as having the same priority. Some 45 per cent who were interviewed said that the Government's main priority was economic issues, only 22 per cent saw the Government as being concerned about poverty and hunger, and only 19 per cent saw it as being primarily interested in reducing the threat of war. The priorities of people do not correspond to the priorities of the Government.
In conclusion, I simply point out that being eleventh out of 21 OECD countries is not good enough for Canada. Other countries such as Denmark, France, the Netherlands, Sweden and Norway have all reached and surpassed the .7 per cent goal. These are countries that take good care of their people. Mediocrity in the face of 800 million people who go to bed hungry every night, if they have a bed, is not good enough for Canada. I urge all Members to give their support to this goal that has widespread support among Canadians. We should urge the Government to bring in legislation to establish .7 per cent of our GNP for development assistance, that that be done by legislation and not left to government whims.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations

speechtext:
I hear barking on the other side of the House.
Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that in a democratic system we must have fair Government and we must have sound financial management.
Mr. Speaker, we are still committed, but as long as we do not have the requisite budget and budget items and as long as we cannot reconcile this with the budgetary measures to which we are committed, I cannot vote in favour of this proposal at this time.
Our commitment remains, and we will meet that commitment and let Canadians-in fact they did so for the famine in Ethiopia-take the lead and encourage them in a positive movement towards increased aid for the countries concerned.
We have two options. As far as the economy is concerned, we promised to restore the confidence of the people in our system, Mr. Speaker. Either we go on like that, or we ask Canadians to tighten their belts. Obviously, I intend to argue against the second option, which asks Canadians to tighten their belts, since that is the one they have chosen.
Had the first option been chosen, Mr. Speaker, what would have happened in a few years? If you examine the federal budget you can see that the last few years were highlighted by a drastic increase in public expenditures and a sharp rise in the budget deficit, which led to an immediate increase in interest rates and the inflation rate. If this trend continues, Mr. Speaker, it will be easy to tell Canadians: Not to worry about next year, the deficit will grow to $60 billion, then to $90 billion the year after. That is the easy way to administer the country. But what is going on, and why indeed can our country grow richer or become poorer? It is strictly a matter of confidence. The Canadian currency, the Canadian economy, it is just like any other market where supply and demand principles prevail.
When foreigners want to invest in Canada, what is their first question? Is this a serious country? Is this a country which has control over its economy? If the answer to those two questions is not affirmative, they go elsewhere. They want their investment to be profitable. Mr. Speaker, this is why certain countries are closed tight to foreign investments: people have lost confidence in the economy, the administration or the policy of those countries. So we could have opted for the first method and said: Let us spend our way out of this mess. In other words, a larger share of our revenues would have been earmarked for debt servicing. But, Mr. Speaker, the more we do that, the heavier the deficit grows, the more we have to tax Canadians. We decided to go for the second method.
We told the people: Let us tighten our belts. And when we ask people to tighten their belts, we expect the Government to do the same, and this applies to external aid as well. What this actually means, Mr. Speaker, is that we have to learn to do more with our limited financial resources. We have had examples of this, you referred to the Ethiopian crisis a moment

June 17, 1986
Official Developmental Aid
ago, it is true, a striking example where with less money we managed to convince Canadians to contribute more, and this has a significant driving and collective impact on international aid. It is the method advocated by the Government at this time. There is something else we said-they keep referring to our broken promises-one of the thing we promised was to restore sound management, a balanced economy and fair government.
Can we tell people today, and I know the Hon. Member would object, that we will no longer index family allowances, we will no longer index old age security pensions for the first 3 per cent as well, and that we will spend more on external aid? If we ask Canadians to tighten their belts, I think we should also ask people outside our country to tighten their belts, and in the final instance we will have to find new ways of making our money more productive. That is how society works and that is also how a just society works. Mr. Speaker, the lower interest rates and lower inflation rate we are enjoying today, something which benefits all Canadians, remain in the eyes of some people just the Government's doing. But it is not just the Government's doing, it is thanks to the renewed confidence of all Canadians and of outside investors in the Canadian economy. This means we can make more resources available to the people of this country, in some cases with less financial outlay. That is the kind of solution we have chosen, and I repeat, Mr. Speaker, we are a responsible and a fair Government. I do not want to ask Canadians to make more sacrifices for our economy than other countries have to make. That, Mr. Speaker, is the most important promise that we have kept.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AID ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING A LEVEL OF GNP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I was listening to the Hon. Member, I was reminded of when I was a student, in the days of the former Premier of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis, who had a natural flair for the dramatic turn of phrase. Duplessis, when faced with the external aid proposal made by St. Laurent, then Prime Minister of Canada, remembered the aid he had given to the village of Cabano in the Lower St. Lawrence area which had burnt to the ground. St. Laurent, on the other hand was asking Canadians-this was in the fifties-to realize they had international responsibilities under what was called the Colombo Plan. So Duplessis' slogan became: "Duplessis gives to Cabano and St. Laurent gives to Colombo", to confuse people.
What we must understand today is that the Hon. Member presented this motion because we must remind Canadians that this is our objective. The Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson under whom I had the honour of being elected and of serving as a Member of Parliament, had tabled this UN report which was adopted by Canada in 1970, as the Hon. Member recalled, and we made this our objective: 0.7 of 1 per cent of our Gross National Product would go to external aid.
Due to circumstances, the objective was postponed from 1975 to 1980, at the latest. My party remains committed to achieving this objective as soon as possible. Just because this country is having problems with the economy and the deficit,
and so forth, and I know we are, and I hope it will be temporary, it does not mean we should shirk our international responsibilities.
Not long ago, Canadians reacted with great enthusiasm while Government was hesitant about spending quite considerable sums of money in connection with the famine in Africa. Canadians knew where their responsibilities lay, and the Hon. Member said so himself. It was the Canadian people who pushed the Government. This means that there is in our society a tremendous amount of understanding for these things, and we should not let this understanding for our international responsibilities and international sharing be diverted to the economy or the Budget or the deficit. Because if we do, there will always be people, both in the House of Commons and across the country who will say: They are right, charity begins at home.
It is a very bad principle to start talking about our international responsibility. We must have a goal. The goal which was set and accepted was .7 of 1 per cent of our Gross National Product. If you start attracting the attention of Canadians to our difficulties and deficit, you stand the chance of killing the base of good will which Canadians have recently manifested toward aid for those who have much less than us. It is not enough to pretend that we are going through difficulties in Canada and to reduce our commitment toward the international community and the people who need so much and look toward Canada as a leader.
My colleague who presented the motion reminded us that young Canadians want leadership on this question. The major preoccupation of young Canadians is the hunger in the world. Young Canadians will pay more taxes than I because I am on my way out while they are on their way in. Yet, their commitment is toward hunger in the world. Their second preoccupation is disarmament. We could link disarmament with development if we understood better what disarmament meant and stopped being paranoid that communists are going to rearm, and always trying to be a step ahead of them. What is going on today on the question of armament is pure madness.
I have no hesitation in connecting the two. If we understood the madness of armament versus disarmament and the immense base of money which could be spent on development, we would understand very well that we would have an easier time. Everything is interlinked. You cannot talk about hunger and poverty and then say that the debate is over and that we will now discuss disarmament. That is all interconnected, Mr. Speaker, as you know very well.
The goal should be to remain committed. That is exactly what my colleague has asked. He asks that we reaffirm that commitment. We may not achieve it, but at least we are committed to it, which means that we will work harder. If you reduce your commitment, of course you work less hard to achieve it. The commitment was reaffirmed at the United
June 17, 1986

Nations by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in September, 1984. He said that we are still committed to .7 of 1 per cent. He was greatly applauded. Everyone said that this was a country which understood its commitment, it is in difficulty and yet reaffirms its commitment. They said that was the kind of Canada they liked. Suddenly we say that .7 is difficult and we will make it .6 until 1990. However, it is now .6 until 1995. I am afraid it is going to be .5 by 1995. When you have no goal or vision, it is easier to reduce your commitments.
I suppose that the intention of my colleague from the New Democratic Party today is to ask Members to recommit themselves publicly, to say that regardless of the difficulty they have noticed that Canadians are way ahead of them and that they are recommitting themselves to that goal. I beg of you not to reduce our commitment. We must not postpone what we strongly believe. There are only six Members left in my Party who sat under Pearson. You would, therefore, understand that I am more committed than others because I have followed his policy ever since.
I am not laying blame. I am only begging people to understand. Regardless of how many pockets of poverty there are in our country and regardless of how much temporary difficulty we may have, there is no better country in the world in which to live than Canada. I said that last Friday when I spoke on the emergency debate on South Africa. People expect leadership from Canada on the issue of apartheid in South Africa. People expect leadership from us. The Government's own polls show that. The youth of the country are committed. They understand the commitment. They will pay taxes much longer than us.
There is no doubt that we can link aid and disarmament. We must understand that any country to which Canada is providing leadership is going through much greater difficulty than Canada has ever known. We must understand that those we help and co-operate with today are the partners of tomorrow. That is something to reflect on. You do not throw money away. You do not exchange technology. You create future partnerships with people who have less than you. That is the message for those who are strictly business-oriented. I am not, but I am practical. I understand that for some people that is their commitment. I think of them as future partners in development for people who have nothing.
Please, I beg of Members to understand the meaning of the resolution put forward by my friend, which is to publicly recommit ourselves to that goal. It should remain the goal of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. I thank my colleague for having introduced the motion. It is very timely and worth while. The idea of introducing legislation to set aid levels is interesting and unique. Obviously it is no guarantee that Governments will set appropriate targets. All
Official Developmental Aid
we need do is look at the present debate on Established Programs Financing.
The Government is moving in the direction of cutting back on transfer payments to the provinces for education, health and human development in Canada. In fact the Government has just moved closure on that legislation, so it is moving very quickly in that direction. However, even though it is possible for a mean-spirited Government whose priorities are not well placed to ignore the human development needs on this globe, that does not mean that legislation like this would not be a useful vehicle in setting goals for international aid. It would certainly give these programs more permanency than they have right now.
The goal of .7 per cent of GNP for international aid was set by the UN so it is an international goal. We should associate ourselves with it in order to show solidarity with the aspirations of all peoples around the globe for the development of the individual and community. It is a minimal obligation to which we can tie ourselves.
The most striking aspect of international development aid, at least to me, is the comparison between the amount of money we spend in that direction compared with the amount we spend on armaments. If we could transfer but a fraction of the money we spend on arms to spending on human development and international aid, we could make a real difference. We could improve the quality of the accommodation people live in and the quality of water they drink. We could eradicate forever a number of diseases with just a fraction of the money which goes to armaments. To move money from our military budgets to our development budgets requires that we find ways to resolve peacefully those conflicts which break out on this planet.
While it is important for us to urge the Government to adopt the goal of .7 per cent of GNP for international aid, it is also important to impress upon people the need to provide leadership in peaceful conflict resolution. It is only when we have found the means for resolving conflicts among nations in a peaceful way that people will feel comfortable about putting down their arms. Therefore, this Government should be taking a direct leadership role on the international stage in order to promote conflict resolution.
Another area of interest is the involvement of Canadians in the international arms race. Not only are private companies selling arms on the international market, arms which are bought by military dictatorships and used to repress their people and block human development, more than that, our tax dollars are supporting that kind of trade. My tax dollars, your tax dollars, the tax dollars of those watching this program tonight go to support the arms trade. We are investing public funds in companies so that they can further promote the sale of arms on the international market. This is tragic to say the least. It is obscene. The Government has announced legislation dealing with pornography; it is too bad it did not have the vision to think of the obscene international arms trade and the

June 17, 1986
Official Developmental Aid
direct role the Canadian Government plays in that area by subsidizing our arms trade.
We have brought before this House on a number of occasions examples of where the Canadian Government has been supporting military trade with Chile. Military arms sold to that country are inevitably used in repressing dissent. Therefore, if we are to reach the objective of international aid, then we have to get this country out of the business of subsidizing the arms trade. We have to use those dollars to encourage companies to undertake other types of economic activity. We know from numerous studies that if companies get involved in other kinds of economic activities, they produce more jobs. We would get a better return for the public dollar invested.
It is important to remind the Government of the international goal of .7 per cent of GNP for international trade. It is important for this Government to be reminded that it needs to set its priorities on the basis of what Canadians want. I cannot quote any specific public opinion poll, but I know from talking to people in my community of Winnipeg that the vast majority of Canadians want action on international development. They want Canadians to be in the forefront of promoting justice on this planet through human development. The Government should be setting those priorities on the basis of what Canadians want rather than on the basis of some other set of priorities.
I think I see you signalling that my time is coming to a quick end, Mr. Speaker. I just want to say that I congratulate my colleague for having brought forward this resolution. It is a creative idea for bringing home to this Government the fact that it needs to place a much higher priority on international development and that Canadians want it to do so. It is the responsibility of the Government to respond and this is a creative way of saying that.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AID ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING A LEVEL OF GNP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Member who has introduced this motion which focuses our attention on one of the most compelling issues that confront humanity. As so often happens, perhaps the most important subject that the House will debate today has been the program for Private Member's Hour. I thank the Member and those associated with him who have made this the primary concern of all of us during this hour together. It is right for them to remind us that the people of Canada share this concern with all of us.
One of the results of the recently concluded study of foreign policy by the Special Joint Committee on Canada's International Relations has been the high priority which the subject of external affairs enjoys throughout the land. It is a priority that has not always been measured within these walls. It has often been assumed that nobody in Canada really cares about foreign policy. That may have been true at one time, but we live in the age of the global village and our people are fully conscious of their belonging to one world. Therefore, people are fully aware of the need for Canada to address the problems
of the world if we are to do justice to our own needs as a nation.
I welcome this opportunity to discuss foreign aid and overseas development. I have to put before the House a concern that the presenter of the motion, and the Member who spoke in support of it, have been guilty nonetheless of certain fallacies; one of them being the fallacy of not relating the necessity to generate wealth in order to provide humanitarian assistance and social development.
One of the most striking fallacies of which we can be guilty of in this chamber is the failure to recognize the need to generate adequate wealth if we are to afford those programs and services without which our life as a people would be poorer, and without which the life of the human race throughout the world would be poorer. It amazes me to hear Members on the other side of the House urge on us one spending program after another, and at the same time oppose efforts that are designed to increase the wealth of this country so that we can possibly afford those spending programs. We often become very superior and very sophisticated about business, industry and commerce. These are in contrast to the intellectual, the cultural, the social activities which are so much more worthy of the mind and the spirit of men and women.
I have to draw to your attention that one Member of the House earlier this afternoon was pleading for funds for the erection of a ballet theatre in the City of Toronto. Now, without the kind of wealth that we hope our burgeoning, booming economy can generate how would such a cultural centre ever be a possibility? We have to keep that in mind whenever we are tempted to close our eyes to the priority of economic concerns. That is equally true when we are talking about overseas aid and foreign development.
The only way by which this country can possibly have the surplus to share with the underdeveloped, with the have-not nations of the world, is by sufficiently generating the wealth that provides that surplus. If all we can produce in this country is that which is required for our subsistence and survival as a people, we have nothing to share. It is only when we have a booming economy, it is only when we have our deficit under control, it is only when we have an economically sound country that we can possibly have something to share with other countries.
I would hope that in the interests of human betterment and overseas aid we would find support for our deficit control policies for they are designed to give us, once again, the surplus that can lift the level of life in this country, and lift the level of life beyond our borders. I point out that our first need as a people, as a parliament, as a government, is to generate the wealth without which our progress as people will be impossible. That is the first fallacy that I noted in the remarks.
The second fallacy is the fallacy of being insensitive to the need for recognizing that simply spending money overseas can be as unproductive as spending it at home. Mention was made
June 17, 1986

of Prime Minister Pearson, for whom we all share an admiration. I recall the war on poverty that he began. He initiated a spending program that people throughout the country supported because of our desire to follow the Government in ending poverty within this land. So year after year the spending continued and mounted and so did the poverty statistics. The intention was worthy, the objective was noble, the effort was admirable, but the results are still there. We now have more people below the poverty level than we had when the war on poverty began. This is true not only in Canada.
Only the other night I read about how this is the sad experience of the people of Sweden. Sweden, of all places, the darling of all the social democrats, that gem of a country, the model that we should all follow. Sweden has now discovered that they have more people below the poverty line than they had 20 years ago. They now have to reassess their approach, not because they have less concern for the poor than they had, but because they are recognizing, as we are recognizing, that you simply do not spend your way into human betterment. We have to recognize that the answer to the needs of the people in the underdeveloped parts of the world lies not simply in our increasing the amount of money we spend there, but lies more in our joining with them in those programs, in those methods by which they will achieve the good life to which they aspire.
For example, in a recent editorial in the London Times, and it is certainly in the parliamentary tradition to quote the Times, and I do so with reference to an editorial called "Africa Help for Self-Help", the Times argues quite rightly that if the level of life in Africa is to be raised it will be raised, solely when the countries of Africa attract, once again, investment capital, in contrast to their failure of recent years. Only 3 per cent of the overseas investment capital of the world has gone into African countries in recent times. So the Times, understandably, urges the Governments of Africa to adopt those policies that once again could attract private investment and join with private investment within the borders of their own countries.
I speak of that because I believe that we have to address ourselves as a Parliament and as a Government to linking our overseas aid with certain developments within the receiving countries, that joined with our aid it will add to the betterment of life within those borders. One of them has been suggested in previous speeches in criticism of military spending. I hope that all Members of Parliament will be conscious of the waste of resources on military spending within so many underdeveloped countries and that we might join together in improving those programs that will lift the level of life. Surely that is the goal of us all.

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking to Motions Nos. 17, 18, 19 and 20. Motion No. 17 would ensure that before the decision is made to hold a prisoner beyond the eligibility date for mandatory supervision, until warrant expiry, the prisoner would be entitled to a hearing. I think that in making such a fundamental decision, which has been held by the courts to be a decision that does involve the liberty of the subject and for which counsel should be present, the individual surely has a right to a hearing. That is the purpose of Motion No. 17. I hope that it will have the support of Members of this House.
Motions Nos. 18, 19 and 20 collectively, when linked with Motion No. 16, would ensure that there are more frequent reviews of an individual who has been gated by the National Parole Board. As it stands now, that review process would only happen once a year. That is simply not good enough. There should be a more frequent review in view of the fact that, once again, we are dealing with the liberty of the subject. I mention the importance of the need for a review process here, a process by which the prisoner affected might be heard.
The statistics show that the record of the National Parole Board with respect to prediction of violence leaves a great deal to be desired. I now have the specific illustration of that. On many occasions we have been told about the fact that between 1975 and 1979 some 52 people were killed by prisoners who had been released on mandatory supervision. Of that number, 31 were the victims of murder, and 21 were the victims of manslaughter. That represents the following percentage of the total releases on mandatory supervision: 1.2 per cent of all those released on mandatory supervision were involved in murder, and .8 per cent were involved in manslaughter. Of the prisoners released on parole, as opposed to mandatory supervision-in other words those released at the discretion of the National Parole Board-we have the following figures:
nine of the prisoners who were released on parole betwen 1975 and 1979 were convicted of murder and a further nine were convicted of manslaughter, for a total of 18 individuals. However, because the numbers involved on parole were much smaller than for those released on mandatory supervision, the actual percentage was higher. It was 1.3 per cent.
What do we have? We have a situation in which a larger percentage of those who are released on parole at the absolute discretion of the National Parole Board are involved in crimes of homicide as opposed to those who are released automatically on mandatory supervision. What does that say about the ability of the National Parole Board to predict violent crime? It very clearly says that the board has been a failure. We are giving this body, which has so demonstrably failed in its duty, even more discretion and even more power to detain people when it has been admitted without any hesitation whatsoever, and without any doubt, that it has a bad record, and when it has been admitted that violence cannot be predicted.
It is for this reason that, among others, a major campaign was launched out of the prison at Collins Bay by the John Howard Society, Collins Bay Chapter, to abolish mandatory supervision. It was called the one-cent campaign. I personally received hundreds and hundreds of envelopes bearing one-cent stamps which urged the Government to abolish mandatory supervision.
Given the fact that we are wasting millions of dollars on a program which has been proved to be ineffective, and which results in such bitterness and such anger among prisoners who believe that they have been denied their earned remission, I believe that is a recommendation that should be very seriously looked at.
I note as well that it is a recommendation supported by, among others, the John Howard Society, the St. Leonard's Society, many distinguished professors of law and criminology, the Canadian Association for the Prevention of Crime, the Elizabeth Fry Society, and many other concerned Canadians. I hope that the Government will accept these motions, which would certainly move some distance toward ensuring adequate due process in a very Draconian system of designating individuals to remain behind bars after they have earned their remission.

He said: Mr. Speaker, these two motions deal with the very important issue of what information must be provided to a prisoner before his or her hearing on parole or before his or her hearing with respect to a decision on gating. As it now stands, the Bill would allow vital information, key information, with respect to this decision to be provided to an inmate or a prisoner, or any other person, by the board before the commencement of, or during, a hearing held pursuant to the provisions of the Act. It is simply not good enough to suggest that a prisoner come into a hearing-such an important hearing on parole or one with respect to gating-and not have any information until he or she literally arrives at the hearing and is told: "Look. Here is the information that we intend to share with you". I say "share" because the National Parole Board has this euphemism of "oral sharing" of information during hearings.
The amendment in Motion No. 22 would delete paragraph (e). The combined effect of these two motions would be to ensure that prisoners are entitled to any information which will be the basis of a decision of the National Parole Board before the hearing and that they have that information at least 15 days before the hearing. I think that that is an elementary and natural form of justice. I hope that the Government will recognize the importance of this particular proposal.
I would like to point out that the provisions with which we are dealing, and particularly "gating", have been described by

June 17, 1986

the former Chairman of the National Parole Board, Mr. William Outerbridge, in the following way:
-it's a brutal tool, it is a clumsy tool and it is a Band-Aid, because it only helps us for a short period of time.
That is the law we are being asked to adopt in Parliament today. In fact, I think we would be doing a disservice to our constituents were we to adopt this law which clearly would result in an increase in the level of violence in our community.
As well, since we are dealing with information provided to prisoners, I would like to take this opportunity to read a letter which was sent to me by a prisoner at the Bowden Institution in Alberta, a letter which touches directly on this point. It reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am incarcerated in Bowden Institution in Alberta, finishing an eleven and a half years sentence which started in May 29/75. I have been incarcerated several times in Canadian Institutions starting in 1958, Kingston, Collins Bay, Joyceville and several farm camps.
I have seen so many changes over the last 27 yrs, actually living conditions have improved two hundred per cent, but at the same time violence has increased four times as much on the inside, it seems as institutions increase security, inmates increase their hostilities and people become more dangerous, not because they were actually dangerous to start with, but because their surrounding becomes more hostile. I've known many inmates who while serving sentences for non-violence, have come involved in stabbing and murders while inside.
One thing that is definitely going to increase the violence inside prisons is by the Government bringing in these changes to the Mandatory Parole Act, which actually places an inmate on an indefinite sentence, the Parole Board having the power to take part or all one's remission, if inmates have nothing to lose then look out. I can see prison officials not liking an individual and have the power to have that person incarcerated as long as the sentence is, and also the Prisons & Parole Boards using this power to produce more informers on the inside and on the outside of Prisons. The courts have been well aware for years when sentencing offenders that they received remission on their sentences for good behaviour, but now giving the Parole Board such great Powers over people is terrible, regardless if we are outcast or not.
By Parliamentary act the Parole Board is even untouchable by our Supreme Courts. The Institution now have the power to take remissions when a prisoner misbehaves, for each time he faces charges they can take remission if the charge is serious, they can take them to outside court, but to wait until the mandatory date approaches, and then to tell the prisoner he is one of those chosen, to have to do the remainder of his remission in the Institution, Boy! I just hope Parliament is willing to accept the consequences, many prisoners are a little emotionally screwed up now, but that will be nothing compared to what they will be.
I certainly wouldn't envy anyone working in Federal Institutions, and there will definitely be more killings and violence amongst prisoners and staff.
It all seems strange when people who make the rules actually don't really know what's happening.
I am finished my sentence on October 21, 1985, and will be on my way. It's just too bad the Solicitor General couldn't of spent even one year in here to know what he's talking about.
That is a very serious letter from a prisoner who has had considerable experience within the system. His views are echoed by prisoners from across Canada. The Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs made the same point.
The whole premise of this legislation is that somehow we will protect our community from dangerous individuals. However, if we are not doing that but only delaying the release of those individuals and at the same time significantly
increasing the level of tension within institutions, then of course we are dealing with a potential time bomb.
The motions which are before the House attempt to introduce an element of basic due process in the hearing system and attempt to ensure that there is a hearing before the review and that before the hearing takes place, the individual is provided in writing with all of the information which is the basis of the decision. These are motions which I hope the House will support.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary could clarify the purpose of the motion moved by the Government, as has been our practice to this point.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Section 15.31 of the Parole Act, the CSC is required to refer a potential detention case to the board not later than six months before the inmate's presumptive release date.
Section 15.33 allows the Commissioner to refer a case within the six-month period under limited circumstances because of new information or changed circumstances. Upon proclamation of the Bill there may be inmates, whose presumptive release date is less than six months away, who should be referred to the board but do not fit the conditions defined in Section 25.33.
It is the intention of the Government that the detention provisions of the Bill be effective immediately upon proclamation. Correctional authorities must be able to refer inmates from a detention review hearing within the first six months of operation if public safety is at stake. Consequently, we are moving that a traditional provision be added to the Bill to allow clearly the referral of potential detention cases within the first six months. Any such referral will have to be made as soon as practicable, and the procedures normally applicable to the review will apply with such modifications as circumstances require.

Mr. Speaker, having heard that explanation, it is quite clear that what we are doing is streamlining justice in the interest of time. I am totally opposed to the provision which is being suggested by the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) in the amendment before us. It is important to note that if we are serious about dealing with the concern about the violence in our communities, and if we are serious about dealing with the very real problem of violent crime, this Bill and the approach taken in it are fundamentally wrong and misguided. Surely we should be looking at the causes of violent crime. We should do, to the greatest extent possible, what we can to eradicate the causes of violent crime. However, the Government does nothing whatsoever to deal with that factor.
As well, it is important to examine conditions within our federal prison system and to recognize that conditions in many cases are appalling. It was in 1976-77 that a special subcommittee of Parliament unanimously recommended that unless there were major changes within the prison system, further crises would in fact erupt. A number of recommendations were made in respect of using imprisonment as a last possible resort. Instead, we sentence people to some of the longest sentences in the western world. Our sentences are far too long, and far too many people are in prison. It should be very clearly set out in
the Criminal Code that prison should be the last possible resort for a judge and should only be used when all else fails. Surely the rule of law should apply within prison walls as well as outside prison walls. We have seen too many instances, whether it be at Kingston Penitentiary or elsewhere, where prison officials arbitrarily ignore the law, whether it be commissioners' directives, criminal law or other law.
The purpose of this grouping of amendments is to ensure that the decision to revoke an individual's liberty is not made by a person appointed by the chairperson of the National Parole Board, but at the very least is made by a justice of the peace. In any other deprivation of liberty clearly it should be and must be a justice of the peace or an independent judicial officer, as opposed to some person designated by the chairperson of the National Parole Board, who is given the power to arrest and detain an individual for some considerable length of time. I would hope that the Government would recognize the importance of this series of amendments and move to accept it.
In looking at the whole issue of prevention, as I mentioned earlier we pay lip service to it within the prison system. There are totally inadequate work programs; some of the best work programs have been shut down. Prisoners themselves are the first people to say that they want to work. They want the right to work in institutions, not just on meaningless, mindless drudgery, but on real jobs which will provide them with skills to help them to obtain jobs outside prison.
There may be Conservative Members who want to speak in this debate. I would welcome their participation. However, I note the hypocrisy of the Government's approach in saying that it wants to cut down on violent crime, but at the same time starves institutions of resources for dealing with prisoners who may in fact be violent. Recent figures have shown that there are only 65 psychologists working in all federal penitentiaries in Canada. Many institutions have fewer than three of them on staff. For example, Kingston Penitentiary with over 400 prisoners, many of whom have serious problems, has twotime psychologists. Instead of this backward approach which will increase the level of violence in our communities, why do we not get serious about prevention? Why do we not recognize that we need more resources within institutions to deal with sex offenders, those offenders with psychological and personal problems. Instead, we have seen the federal Government cutting back on programs for sex offenders. The case-loads of psychologists within institutions are absolutely enormous. Basically, handling units have very serious problems and are completely unable to cope with them, given the resources which they now have.
I reject the approach taken in this legislation, as do my colleagues. We suggest that it is about time the Government took seriously its mandate to prevent violent crime, not to increase the possibility of violent crime through legislation such as this. I call upon the Government to adopt the motions which are now before the House.

speechtext: I remind Hon. Members that the motions will be grouped for debate and voted on separately.

Mr. Speaker, in many ways these two motions go to the heart of this Bill and deal with a very fundamental issue. Very briefly, the issue is whether this legislation is to operate retroactively or to apply from the date upon which it is proclaimed. As the Bill is now worded, it would apply to those prisoners who are already incarcerated as well as to those who were sentenced after the adoption of this legislation. In my view it is profoundly unjust and unfair to apply this legislation to prisoners who are already in institutions having been sentenced under a particular regime and then denied the right to which they should be entitled, the benefit of the earned remission that they have accrued during that sentence.
The prisoners that we are talking about were sentenced by judges who were well aware of the provisions of the Criminal
Code and various parole Acts affecting sentence. There have been a variety of court cases on this point. It is very clear that judges have taken this into consideration in determining the appropriate length of sentence. Indeed, in the British Columbia Court of Appeal it was held that remission and parole are proper matters for consideration in the determination of sentence in appropriate cases.
A recent study on sentencing by Professor John Hogarth dealt with this important question. In that study provincial court judges were asked to indicate whether they adjusted their sentences in light of the possibility of parole being granted or, presumably, mandatory supervision. Two out of three judges who were interviewed admitted that they did increase the length of sentence imposed. The majority of provincial court judges admit that they evade the directions of the Ontario Court of Appeal on this matter.
This means the prisoners who are now in federal institutions have been sentenced to terms of imprisonment based upon the existing provisions of mandatory supervision and parole. We are now changing the rules in midstream. We are telling those prisoners that even though they were sentenced on the basis of a previous regime, we are going to apply the new rules to them as well. I suspect that that is in breach of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of Canada as well as being fundamentally unfair, unjust and unworkable.
This point was made by many witnesses who appeared before our committee. For example, the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies pointed out that the detention order could be applied to all prisoners regardless of whether they were convicted before or after the coming into force of the Act. As they said, it is blatantly unjust to prisoners to apply retroactively measures with such potentially serious repercussions.
We have the views of the John Howard Society of Canada. They say that Section 11 (i) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides that no accused can be sentenced to a higher punishment merely on account of a legislative increase in penalty after commission of the crime but before sentence. In other words, increased penalties cannot be applied retroactively. The John Howard Society also refers to Section 7 of the Charter. It seems clear, therefore, that applying the gating order provisions to prisoners who are already serving their sentences and have earned their remission before the passage of the legislation is a blatant violation of Section 11 (i) and Section 7 of the Charter.
Finally on this point, the Canadian Bar Association and the Criminal Lawyers Association said:
Our associations are particularly concerned with the retroactivity of these various legislative proposals .... Simply put, these sections would make the new regime of "gating" and "one shot mandatory" applicable to persons who have already been sentenced.
They continue:
Is this Committee assured that Sections 5 and 12 of Bill C-67 will survive attacks based on Sections 7 or 15 of the Charter? Is it fair for Parliament to change the rules without some prior notice?

Do you not face the very real possibility that many prisoners will now decline release on mandatory supervision entirely, particularly with regard to the findings of the Ouimet Committee to the effect that at that time only about 60 per cent of eligible prisoners applied for parole because prisoners "prefer to complete their sentence in the institution rather than place their-remission period in jeopardy"?
These are grave issues of justice and liberty. Once again the Government has said that it does not care about those provisions and is prepared to apply the whole thing retroactively-
In the House of Commons in the United Kingdom in July of 1910 Winston Churchill put it very clearly. He said:
The mood and temper of the public with regard to the treatment of crime and criminals is one of the most unfailing tests of the civilization of any country.
I suggest that if we adopt the legislation now before the House we as a Parliament and a nation will have failed that test, not only from the perspective of prisoners but also from the perspective of the communities which we represent and from the perspective of the victims of crime. I, therefore, urge the Government to accept this amendment and to ensure that we are not harshly applying these rules retroactively but that if they must come into effect we apply them from the date that the legislation is proclaimed.

Motion No. 30
That Bill C-67, be amended by deleting Clause 11.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Motion No. 30 which is now before the House is to delete Clause 11 of this Bill. Clause 11 is the clause which would implement a scheme of denying earned remission to those individuals whose mandatory supervision has been revoked when those individuals fall within a particular category set out in the legislation. This so-called one shot mandatory supervision will have a very serious impact on the population of our prison system which is overcrowded. Indeed, the correctional investigator was recently very critical of the federal penitentiary system in that it double-bunks prisoners. To the extent that this Bill is going to add to the population of our prison system, it will obviously cause very significant problems.
I would also note that as the Bill is now worded it would deny earned remission to those prisoners whose mandatory supervision is revoked merely as a result of the contravention of terms or conditions of "mandatory". The Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee unanimously recommended that this should not be the case. I refer to their interim report to the Senate of May 14, 1986. They are referring to one shot mandatory supervision, in other words, the denial of the right to earn further remissions to certain inmates whose mandatory supervision has been revoked.
I might pause here to note that the whole concept of earned remission has been strongly supported by prison guards as well as by prisoners. It provides some incentive for good behaviour in the institutions. As it stands now, if you are not eligible for earned remission then there is no incentive for good behaviour. If we eliminate earned remission for these prisoners we will simply make them that much more likely to cause problems and aggravate tensions in the institutions. They have absolutely nothing to lose.
The Senate committee said that the scope of the amendment on mandatory supervision was considerably narrowed in the legislative committee. Only inmates who have been made the subject of formal consideration for detention under the Bill, but who are not detained by order of the board, are to lose the right to earn further remission on reincarceration following revocation of their release on mandatory supervision. This amendment, however, fails to take into account the criticism that an inmate may have his release revoked for contravention of terms and conditions of that release which have nothing whatever to do with his or her perceived or potential dangerousness. Even the narrow class of inmates who would become subject to the one shot amendment should not lose the right to

June 17, 1986
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
earn remission by reason of a technical or minor breach of conditions which results in revocation. That right should only be lost if there is a criminal conviction while on release.
How can Members of the House disagree with that unanimous recommendation of Liberal and Conservative Senators? After all, if mandatory supervision is revoked because an individual travels more than 25 miles beyond the area in which he is supposed to be residing, or if he has a drink when he should not, or if he takes out a line of credit when he is not supposed to take out, we are going to throw the person in jail. Not only that, they will not have any opportunity to earn remission on the remainder of their sentence. That must surely constitute cruel and unusual punishment.
In addition to that, it will add to overcrowding of institutions. What we have proposed is that if this one shot mandatory supervision is to apply, at least make sure it applies only where an individual has been involved in criminal activity, not where he has merely breached a term or condition of his mandatory supervision. That is the reason, among others, that we have suggested that this provision in Clause 11 be deleted. I hope Members of the House will support this very reasonable and modest proposal.

Motion No. 33:
That Bill C-67 be amended in Clause 13 by striking out lines 40 to 43 at page 18 and lines 1 to 16 at page 19 and substituting the following therefor:
13.(1) Three years after the coming into force of sections 15.2 and 15.6 of the Parole Act and the schedule thereto as enacted by sections 5 and 8 respectively of this Act and subsections 24(3) to (5) and section 24.11 of the Penitentiary Act as enacted by subsection 10(2) and section 11 respectively of this Act shall cease to be in force.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 33, which is now on the floor for debate, would provide in effect for a sunset clause within this legislation. Many of us would argue that the sun should not rise with this particular legislation, but at the very least if it does rise it should set three years after it comes into effect. That is precisely what the purpose of this motion is. It would provide that the sections in question, the heart of this Bill, would cease to be of any force or effect three years after the coming into force of the Bill.
What that would do is to ensure that the Government puts substance into its promise that it intends to undertake a comprehensive review of correctional law. This review is long overdue. It has been ten years since Parliament last examined the whole question of corrections and prisons in our country, and what we have seen is a prison system which has grown out of control.
It is a system in which prisons are built not on the basis of correctional criteria, but built on the basis of patronage, such as Port Cartier Prison, which by sheer coincidence happens to be located within the Prime Minister's constituency, or Renous Penitentiary, which was built by the previous Government on exactly the same socio-economic conditions, pork-barrelling to help a Liberal Member in New Brunswick.
We believe the time has come for a very fundamental review. Even the Nielsen task force said that it was about time that we recognized that the S800 million plus a year that we are spending on corrections should be reviewed. We are sending far too many people to prison in this country and not using alternatives to imprisonment, wherever possible. We are not emphasizing prevention of crime, which is so fundamental.
The legislation before us which would be the subject of a sunset clause contains many very serious implications, the first one being the loss of inmates' earned remission and the possibility of any earned remission. Second, I would note that prisoners who were incarcerated prior to the passage of the Bill would automatically and arbitrarily have their sentences basically increased by one-third because of the fact that judges will not have taken into consideration in sentencing the fact that an individual would serve the total amount of time.
It would grant new quasi-judicial powers to the National Parole Board when we have seen clearly that it has not used the powers which it has with any great degree of wisdom. Judicial powers are the mandate of the courts, and not the mandate of a Parole Board which has been appointed by the Government of the day, and the members of which in too many cases have been appointed on the basis of partisan
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
political considerations. We have seen a lot of former Members of Parliament who finally found their resting place on the National Parole Board. Surely that is not acceptable with a body which has such sweeping quasi-judicial and judicial powers.
The Bill will lead to an increase in tension between and among inmates and penitentiary staff, which may increase the level of violence within institutions. It will lead to overcrowding, which may also lead to such violence because of increased stress and the total absence of any meaningful programs within the penitentiary system. It will lead to increased psychological damage to prisoners and their families. It will lead to an increase in the level of violence in our communities due to the fact that the prisoners who have been designated as the most dangerous of all are going to be released directly on to the street without any form of surveillance whatsoever.
I would note as well that the Elizabeth Fry Society in Halifax pointed out that a Government which endorses a free enterprise system should not consider the counterproductive measure of removing all incentives from confined human beings. As they say, the increased anxiety and bitterness generated among the inmates who will have their rights denied by the passage of this Bill increases the potential of even more violence in society once these embittered people are released from the human warehouses in which they now find themselves.
The suggestion that there be a sunset clause is not one which is particularly radical. The Senate unanimously recommended such a sunset clause. The Standing Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs in the report to which I referred earlier recommended that. It said the following:
The fourth and final issue has to do with the duration of this proposed legislation, and the process by which it should be reviewed. The Solicitor General has indicated that Bill C-67 is in many respects a stop-gap measure intended to deal with some pressing issues pending a more thorough revision of corrections legislation in the near future.
The last time we heard about a stop-gap measure which was just a temporary measure pending more fundamental review was on the prostitution legislation. Members of the House remember that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) said that Bill C-49 is a stop-gap measure, an interim step, and he promised that he would be bringing in more comprehensive legislation to deal with the issue of prostitution. Of course the Government got cold feet and backed off. The so-called stopgap measure, a repressive sledge-hammer piece of legislation, remains on the books today. It is a piece of legislation which was criticized by the Government House Leader when he was a distinguished member of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee. That legislation is on the books today. It was a stop-gap measure and certainly was not followed by any comprehensive legislation.
That is the fear that we have with this legislation which is now before the House. We are told it is a stop-gap measure, but we know very well that it is likely to be the end and not the beginning of any meaningful change.

June 17, 1986
Parole and Penitentiary Acts
The Senate recommended that there be a sunset clause and I quote:
committee is of the opinion that the Bill should contain a "sunset" clause which would deem its provision to have no force after a certain date. We would fix that date at five years from the coming into force of the legislation.
Mr. Speaker, they are a fairly conservative body over there so I suggested three years, but the principle of a sunset clause is one which was unanimously supported by the members of the Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs, and I would hope that this House would see the wisdom of supporting a similar provision.
Finally, I just want to draw to the attention of the House an excellent article which was written by Graham Stewart, the Executive Director of the John Howard Society of Kingston and district. His article, which is entitled Mandatory Supervision: Politics and People, sets out very clearly the arguments for abolition of mandatory supervision. Mr. Stewart also appeared before the legislative committee studying this Bill and made very powerful and compelling arguments as to why we should not adopt this backward approach. In the article Mr. Stewart sets out the objectives of mandatory supervision and shows how these objectives have not been realized since it was adopted in 1970. He concludes:
From a correctional perspective, the Committee-
The committee which studied mandatory supervision, a committee established by the Solicitor General-
-could not possibly have produced a more scathingly critical indictment of Mandatory Supervision.
He then suggests:
-the money spent on Mandatory Supervision could be spent much more effectively; first, in demystifying the correctional process for the public, and secondly, by ensuring that housing, employment and family support networks are maintained for inmates and ex-inmates. This action may not satisfy those who seek punitive revenge, but it might do something to save ourselves and our neighbours from being victims of future crimes. That seems reasonable to me.
That seems reasonable to this Member of Parliament and to this Party as well. I suggest that far from saving ourselves and our neighbours from being victims of future crime, if we adopt this legislation we will be adding to the level of violent crime in our society. For that reason I propose that we reject the Bill before the House, that we adopt the sunset clause, and that we come to our senses and recognize that it is time to examine the fundamental approach taken in this country to corrections, correctional law and the prevention of crime.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MARINE ATLANTIC INC. ACQUISITION AUTHORIZATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and say a few words with respect to third reading of this Bill. I understand that some colleagues may want to add a few words about the Bill.
Let me simply indicate to the House that the ferry services in Atlantic Canada have not done a bad job. In fact, they have done a very good job. We have heard that they could do better. We have heard that perhaps the sea lane links to Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland should in effect, be extensions of the Trans-Canada Highway. I must say, as an Atlantic Canadian, that is not a concept that I have opposed. Indeed, it is one that I supported for 25 or 30 years.
The Bill in front of us tonight does not deal with that. It deals with the simplicity of giving form and legal structure to a child of Canadian National Railways, born some seven or eight years ago in the form of CN Marine. At the time, all in this Chamber were agreed that when CN Marine, Incorporated found its feet, found itself in the position of being able to serve Atlantic Canadians in terms of freight, passenger and vehicle traffic between the mainland and the islands and the intercoastal trade, that we would place it in a position of being independent, separate and apart; indeed, we describe it as an entity on its own and a Crown corporation responsible to itself.
There is always a conflict when we ask an agency to respond to the needs of another agency that, in fact, serves an entirely different goal. The matter in front of Your Honour tonight gives body and spirit to that. It gives to the management and employees of CN Marine its own identity. We call it Marine Atlantic, Atlantic Marine, and we do so because it reflects the Atlantic regional nature and concept of the effort and activity of CN Marine. We call it that because in fact it does finally separate it from CN. We do so because we believe that, and so do the employees. They are quite prepared now, today, and tomorrow to stand up on their own, to build for Atlantic Canadians that type of service, that type of facility, that is required by people living in Prince Edward Island and in the great Province of Newfoundland.
We would hope that members of this Chamber would give it expeditious passage. It was dealt with, I must say, with expedition. I must commend the Chairman of the legislative committee. Regretfully, he is not able to be with us this evening. I would commend the members of both opposition Parties for their role in rapidly dealing with this. I would commend them for their very reasonable consideration of evidence that was given to us by the President of CN Marine, who will become the President of Marine Atlantic. I would ask that this matter pass somewhat expeditiously.

I do not want to ever insinuate that I am as great an orator as is my colleague, the Hon. Member for
June 17, 1986

Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), although we share the
same first name.
I would like to briefly speak on Bill C-38. We will not prolong the Bill this evening. Changing the name of CN Marine to Marine Atlantic is not really a significant change. I would like to address the service itself. Ferry service should be made more efficient for the customers. The customers of whom I speak are people from my province, the great Province of Prince Edward Island and also those who visit from other parts of North America, who find themselves, on many occasions, waiting quite extended periods of time in order to get on the ferries. Increasingly, they also find it is becoming more and more expensive.
Almost every year, we see increases in the ferry rates, but we do not see a corresponding increase in efficiency to the travelling public. Not only are we paying more to use the service, but we seem to find, almost annually, fewer and fewer crossings. In my riding, in the last year and a half, I have heard many complaints from truckers. They are taking produce, mainly potatoes, but also some other perishables such as fish, and they must leave at certain times in order to catch the ferry. Some times of the year, certainly in July and August when the tourist traffic is heavy, we find that there are long line-ups. Sometimes they have to wait for two or three crossings before they can actually get their trucks on the ferry, because they are competing with the tourist industry. That delays them. When going to Montreal from Prince Edward Island with a load of fresh fish, three or four hours delay has a tremendous effect on the quality of the product and, if it is too long a delay, can reflect in the price paid back to the producer.
It is very important that the Government not only change the name of CN Marine to Marine Atlantic but that it also insist, in the mandate that is given to this Crown corporation, that it provide the proper kind of service to the travelling public. Of course, if one lives in Cape Tormentine, New Brunswick, where the Borden ferry reaches the mainland, one can get into one's car and drive to Vancouver, British Columbia, without paying any kind of a toll at all on the Trans-Canada Highway or other highways. Unfortunately, if one is from Newfoundland or Prince Edward Island and one leaves Summerside or Charlottetown or Tignish, one must pay the cost of using that ferry, going back and forth.
I have had in the past, and I will have in the future-unless some Government in the future does something about it-some sort of disagreement with that sort of concept. I believe that the residents of the Provinces of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland should have free access on the ferry in order to give everyone right across the country an equal opportunity. It should be the same as it is for those who live in Ontario or Manitoba, or in any other province, where one can drive on the highways without paying for the cost.
Some people have said: "What about Vancouver Island?" I believe it is a different situation on Vancouver Island. If one is
Marine Atlantic Inc.
a British Columbian and comes from Vancouver Island, then one is part of British Columbia. However, that area falls under provincial jurisdiction. All the different islands and areas are tied up making them one province. I make that remark because Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland are somewhat different. I would not say that there should actually be more than one free crossing. However, there should be at least one.
Those are my remarks. I hope that the Government of Canada and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) will not be content to say: "We have done something for CN Marine by changing its name". I hope that they will carry that just a little bit further and insist that this new Crown agency provide the kind of service that is necessary in order to give the people who are living on the two islands an equal opportunity and to make them equal partners with the rest of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in briefly in the debate on Bill C-88, an Act which will carve out Marine Atlantic Inc. from CNR. Before I start I would like to apologize to the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) for having referred to him by the name of one of his colleagues. Perhaps I did it because to someone from central Canada, such as myself, all the folks in Atlantic Canada look the same. I suspect that the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) will begin to look the same as the Hon. Member for Egmont as he adds a few years to his age. I apologize to the Hon. Member.
I find it ironic that we are dealing with third reading of this Bill today. I realize that is not because of any plan-God knows there is no plan in this place these days. It is ironic that on the day that another decision has been announced by Canadian National Railways with respect to a change in services provided in Atlantic Canada, and when we recently saw a carve-out of another arm of CN, that we are today in effect finalizing the fragmentation of that great company known as the CNR. Today we are carving out the marine side, at least as it applies to the ferry service. Earlier today there was an announcement made with respect to the privatization of the Moncton shops, and whatever that may mean.

subtopic: MARINE ATLANTIC INC. ACQUISITION AUTHORIZATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It means we are going to save the jobs in Moncton.

subtopic: MARINE ATLANTIC INC. ACQUISITION AUTHORIZATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member talks about perhaps saving the jobs in Moncton. Time will tell. Perhaps the answer to that question will be determined at the next election, especially in respect to what the people of Moncton think with regard to the decision that was made by CN and, ultimately, by the Government of Canada.
A decision was also made to privatize the CN trucking operation, CN Route. I find it ironic that today of all days we are in the process of finalizing what in theory is just a paper move. We are changing a name. We are changing the ownership from indirect ownership by the Government of Canada to a direct ownership. I am a bit worried about that. I am worried

June 17, 1986
Marine Atlantic Inc.
because I am not sure what the ultimate impact will be on the people of Atlantic Canada. I am not sure that there will be no change, as the Government suggests. The Government suggests that there will be no change in service and no change in the way in which Marine Atlantic Inc. operates vis-a-vis CN Marine.
We have been told that there will be no change in the rates, other than those that are normally applied through inflation. Time will tell. I hope that this move will not have a negative effect on the people of Atlantic Canada. I say that because of my belief in this nation. We would be quite happy if there were a negative change and if it were taken out on the Government of the day. That would help those of us on this side of the House. I do not say that in a partisan way. I strongly believe that what we should be doing is supporting the people of Canada.
The area upon which I would like to focus is an area which has caused the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Forrestall) to have a gleam in his eye for the 20 years or more that he has been in this House. I refer to the extension of the Trans-Canada Highway-
