speechtext: I agree with that.

subtopic: MARINE ATLANTIC INC. ACQUISITION AUTHORIZATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
-to include those vital links to our water-isolated provinces in Atlantic Canada. Someone who lives in northern Ontario can drive from Thunder Bay to Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver without having to pass through a toll booth and without having to pay a specific fee to use a surface transportation link. As a Canadian, that person finds it disgusting to know that the people in Atlantic Canada, who have no choice when it comes to communicating with other parts of this land, have to pay a fee to use that extension of the Trans-Canada Highway.
I moved an amendment in committee which would have ensured that Marine Atlantic Inc. would operate under the same fee structure as the Trans-Canada Highway. In other words, it would operate at no direct charge to the user. Had the Government the fortitude to accept my amendment, it would have united the country in a real way and not just a theoretical one.
In order not to mislead anyone, I want to make it clear that we taxpayers would share even more than we do today in the cost of providing those services. Through our federal tax dollars we would pay for the ease of access from Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland to the mainland to ensure that those Canadians, those residents of those waterbound provinces, would have the same access in the sense that it would not cost them any more than it costs you or I, Mr. Speaker, to reach another part of this great nation.
Obviously, the chance for us to make that change has been lost. Given this Government's fascination with cost recovery and user pay, it is doubtful that under this administration there will be a change for the better. I warn Hon. Members that there will be a change for the worse. As the Conservative
Government applies more and more user fees, the people of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland will have less access to the same services to which we in the rest of Canada have access.
Last Friday I received some information regarding a cost-recovery Bill that was passed in the United States which gives that Government the power to charge for customs services. It gives it the power to charge every truck, every package of mail that goes through customs and every commercial vessel that enters into American waters a fee. This is directly related to the costs of Marine Atlantic and it will come home to roost with this Government.
Every time a ferry docks at Bar Harbour in Maine, it will have to pay $397. That does not seem like very much, but we must look at the frequency of visits to that community. That community in the United States is one which we service though we probably do not have to. However, we do so because it is appropriate and important for the people of the community of Yarmouth that we have that link.
We as Canadians will have to pay more. Marine Atlantic will have to come up with another $66,000 per year in fees that it will have to pay for the service. One of two groups will have to pay for that. It will either be the users through tolls charged by Marine Atlantic or an increase in the subsidies which are already at around 55 per cent. Those subsidies are paid by the taxpayers of Canada.
The Government will have a hard time fighting against the imposition of user fees in the United States because it believes in user fees. It believes that we should draw more and more money from the specific users of a service. It does not believe that we as a nation have a responsibility to provide the infrastructure and the transportation and communication links. The Government will be like a toothless tiger if it goes to Washington to complain about this new fee that will be charged as of July 7.
I know that Government Members from Atlantic Canada understand the negative impact of that kind of approach. I regret that this is the situation in which we find ourselves. I regret the impact that this will have on the users of Marine Atlantic and on the communities in Atlantic Canada.
Before I close, there are a few other things I wish to say. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) was present in the House tonight and perhaps he is watching us now on television. We know that the potato producers in Prince Edward Island do not have any alternatives. If they want to get their produce to market, they have to rely on marine services. Anything that the Government does that will have an impact on their costs will clearly have an impact on their ability not only to sell produce, but to actually receive a return for their labour. I would caution the Government to avoid excesses and to avoid this fantasy it has of getting more money out of the users of
June 17, 1986

these services. Ultimately, this will kill agricultural, commercial, small business and fisheries industries in Atlantic Canada.
We will support Bill C-88. We recognize that it only enacts something which actually happened over a year ago and we accept that. However, I will repeat what I said earlier and that is that we wish the Government had come to Parliament first to have the Bill debated before the carve-out actually occurred. Let us think about that. In the future, legislation should be debated and then things should happen, not the other way around.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly will keep my comments relevant. I go on to say that I can see that Petro-Canada will follow in the footsteps of the CN family of companies.
Nevertheless, I am very pleased to see that CN Marine has been spun away from CN. I hope that will make a difference. I hope that the influence of CN on CN Marine will be broken and that it will not be tied by an umbilical cord of nonsense, impropriety and services which run contrary to the benefit of the people of Canada.
CN Marine has had to bear a very difficult weight on its shoulders by being associated with CN. It has had to pay for
Marine Atlantic Inc.
marshalling services for which it really should not have had to pay, costs which should have been the responsibility of CN Rail. CN likes to say that it was not getting any funding from CN Marine or any of the subsidiaries or from the Government of Canada and that it was totally self-sufficient. It was bleeding enough from companies like CN Marine and VIA Rail to make up for any loss it would ever have had to make up. Of course, VIA Rail is not in question here tonight, but VIA Rail has been stymied even more than CN Marine.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Egmont, has said, the very fact that this name is being changed will not alter the activities of the new company unless the Government gives it proper direction. It will not change unless the Government listens to Canadians and considers the connection between North Sydney and Port aux Basques an extension of the Trans-Canada Highway. The great increases that have recently been put on should stop and the service should be run in the best interests of the people.
The Government recently spent a good deal of money for a new vessel, Caribou, which has good sleeping quarters and can be a very positive feature of the gulf crossing. However, what has CN Marine done? It has put the Caribou on during the day crossing and has put a ferry, which does not have any sleeping accommodations, on the evening runs. Therefore, there is no sleeping capacity in the evening and all sorts of sleeping capacity during the day.
What kind of service are people getting on the gulf crossing? They are waiting for hours. The new vessel, which was supposed to be able to turn around quickly, is leaving port in North Sydney two hours late because the loading ramp and vessel do not coincide. CN Marine originally located in Moncton, and rightfully so. Initially it was a spinoff of CN, and CN has its Atlantic quarters in Moncton. It was only right that it should be located there. However, in addition to having its headquarters in Moncton, this is a company which has a legal office in Halifax and a gulf headquarters in St. John's, Newfoundland. Neither city is served by CN Marine. They are there for political reasons. It is because the Members from those two locations, who are both Ministers of the Government, felt that the Crown corporation should have a presence in their constituencies.
Particularly in the case of St. John's, jobs were taken away from North Sydney and an area of Cape Breton Island with an unemployment rate of approximately 40 per cent. I do not begrudge St. John's, Newfoundland or any other community jobs. However, we should not take from one area of the country to give to another. We should not do so arbitrarily, at the expense of relocating people who have lived in communities all their working lives and of putting them in an area which does not have any relationship to the company through which they will be employed.

June 17, 1986
Marine Atlantic Inc.
Granted, the subsidy for CN Marine is extensive. It has been stated tonight that the subsidy is 55 per cent. Undoubtedly it is a weighty expense for the Government of Canada. However, it is also important to consider service to Canadians. Service to Canadians must be foremost. This is really what CN Marine and the new company, Marine Atlantic Inc., must be all about. In addition to the subsidy, the Government of Canada is paying to Atlantic Container Express, which ships directly from Montreal to St. John's, a subsidy of millions of dollars per year to compete against CN Marine. What will be the result of this? Because Atlantic Container Express is being subsidized to compete against CN Marine, CN Marine will lose more money and will have to be further subsidized. Therefore, the private sector and the public sector are both being subsidized by the Government of Canada. However, if we took the subsidy off the private sector, the subsidy to the public sector would be less and Canadians would save millions of dollars per year. This is the burden under which the new company will have to operate. This is the burden of complete inattention and unconcern on the part of the Government for a service on which people in Atlantic Canada must rely.
What is CN Marine doing with regard to public relations in the communities which it is serving? For example, in North Sydney, CN Marine will not do a thing to promote its downtown area. It will not erect a sign indicating where the downtown is located or how one gets there. In fact, it discourages people from leaving their cars and going to the downtown area of North Sydney, although it is only a few hundred feet away.
These people are waiting for hours in their cars to take the ferry to Newfoundland, and CN Marine and the Government of Canada have provided nothing for them to do while they are waiting. It is really a case of discouraging people from taking the ferry service. It is not that they could take an alternate service, but it has a direct bearing upon Newfoundland tourism. If people hear about long waits and overdue ferry departures, they will be discouraged from taking the service to Newfoundland. In effect, it is discouraging tourism in that province at the same time as the Province of Newfoundland is spending hundreds of thousands of dollars to promote it. The Government of Canada is working contrary to the Province of Newfoundland and acting against the interest of that province.
Also a little game is being played by the federal Government and the Province of Newfoundland. The federal Government, through CN, is discussing the possibility of closing completely the rail line in Newfoundland. The Province of Newfoundland is saying that it does not want that. One of the terms of union in 1949 was that the rail line would be maintained, and it cannot be closed unless the province gives its permission. Of course there is the question of what the Province of Newfoundland will take for its permission or how much it will accept. That is something we have yet to determine.
One can believe that a figure will be reached because CN is playing its old game of let the services deteriorate until they get so bad that no one will want to use them or they will not be
safe to use. Then a large amount of money will have to be put into this system in order to bring the services up to standard, and no one will be able to afford it. In that event, the province is faced with the likelihood that the service could be closed.
What would be the result of the railway service in Newfoundland being closed? It means that there would only be a short period of time before the next step is contemplated, that is, the closing and shutting down of the rail line between eastern Nova Scotia and Cape Breton Island. This is the secret agenda which CN likes to work over at the expense of people in Atlantic Canada. This is the secret agenda which it denies. This is the secret agenda which it works on and plans toward. Such was the situation in the shops in Moncton. There was no indication or statement with regard to those shops. CN was asked many times what it would do with them. It was announced today that they would be sold to the private sector and that there would be no loss of jobs for the people in Moncton. I should like to know how the federal Government will enforce that. Once the shops are sold, how will the federal Government prohibit the private sector company from reducing the workforce? Once it is sold, it is sold. There is no way unless we get special conditions from the purchaser beforehand, and I do not believe any of these conditions have been obtained.
In closing, I should like to say that the situation in Atlantic Canada in respect of transportation is a very bad one. This Act may or may not have a positive bearing. It remains to be seen. It is largely upon the back of the federal Government to give proper instructions to the new company to operate in the best interest of Atlantic Canadians and to ensure that subsidies are maintained, so that rates are not increased to such an extent that no one will be able to use them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-88. Hon. Members opposite were attempting to distract me from my duty and to prevent me from participating in this final opportunity to try to restore to the House of Commons some sense of sensitivity, understanding, and appreciation of the values which make Canada the kind of country it is. When Hon. Members opposite find the courage, integrity, and backbone to rise in their places to defend this measure, they would have us believe, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Forrestall) attempted a few days ago, that Bill C-88 is a Bill about a change of name for a Crown corporation.
This bill would formalize in law, in legislation, the severing of the relationship between CN Marine and CN that has taken place over the last year. The Parliamentary Secretary and other Members opposite want us to believe that nothing more than a name change in Bill C-88 is what is on the agenda of the House of Commons tonight. Nothing could be further from the truth. Above and beyond simply changing the name
June 17, 1986

of CN Marine to Marine Atlantic Inc., the implications of the Bill are profound for the people of the Atlantic region.
The Government of Canada is asking Members during these dying days of Parliament, when it hopes the people of Canada and Members of this Parliament are not paying attention, to slip through this Draconian measure called Bill C-88 which will force upon the Atlantic region a user-pay philosophy. With one broad sweep of the sword, one foul vicious insensitive and cruel sweep of the sword, the Government of Canada is attempting not only to sever CN Marine from the main company, CN, but it is attempting to impose on the people of Atlantic Canada a user-pay concept that fails to recognize those things that make the Atlantic region of this country unique and different from the country as a whole.
It is interesting to note that Bill C-88 received first reading in the House of Commons in December, 1985. I want you to note that date, December 1985, Mr. Speaker. It was September, 1985 that the ministerial task force on program review, more colloquially and commonly known as the Nielsen task force, the task force of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), submitted its report to the Cabinet of Canada. It was a task force established to assist the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in setting within his Department a program of expenditure reduction.
In September, 1985, that task force looked at the Atlantic region of Canada and said it was possible for the Government of Canada, by walking away from some concepts we hold near and dear in this country, to save some dollars, to alter the bottom line of the ledger of the Government of Canada. That task force, which reported in September, 1985, a scant two months before this measure found its way on to the floor of the House of Commons for first reading said, and I am paraphrasing, that the cost of ensuring that the people of Atlantic Canada would feel, with respect to transportation systems, a sense of being first-class Canadians was a cost too high. The price was too high. The Nielsen task force report recommended that the Government of Canada could achieve substantial savings in the Atlantic region by lowering the level of service to Atlantic Canadians provided under CN Marine by lowering the quality of service and by increasing the rates.
The Government of Canada was so proud of that one year initiative undertaken under the direction of the Deputy Prime Minister that for the first time in the history of Parliament, the Government of Canada did not provide free copies of the report. The Government said to the people that if you want to know what the Deputy Prime Minister is suggesting in all regions, not just Atlantic Canada, for a mere $300 or $400 we will send you a copy of the 27 volumes.
What is the Government attempting? What is the Government doing to reduce the deficit? A Conservative Member said the Government is attempting to reduce the deficit. The Government said it would reduce the deficit by identifying a whole series of programs and government initiatives that represented fat and waste. We on this side of the House, who would endorse such an exercise of cutting fat and waste, have
Marine Atlantic Inc.
been waiting with bated breath for the Government to come forward with a long list of scurrilous and disgusting and wasteful programs.
We have waited in vain because there is no long list. Instead what we have seen is Bill C-96 which would cut $8 billion from [DOT] the national deficit by transferring that $8 billion on to the backs of the provincial Governments. Members and the Canadian public would say what is Bill C-96, what does that officious sounding name denote? It happens to be a Bill that would cut from the health and education programs some $8 billion by transfering that deficit on to the backs of provincial Governments.
In the same vein, with the same insensitive approach, the Government of Canada has produced Bill C-88, a Bill to sever CN Marine from CN, to set up a separate Crown corporation in order to identify the cost of providing that service to Atlantic Canadians and to be able to target better fare increases and system reductions in the Atlantic regions.
Atlantic Canadians being frugal people, and I am proud to say I am an Atlantic Canadian, do not mind any Government cutting the fat away from the system, but when the Government wields the long arm of the sword indiscriminately and slashes through the fat into the muscle and bites deep into the bone straight through to the marrow and bleeds that marrow out of the system-the marrow which is important in preserving the body-then the people of Atlantic Canada begin to wonder about this faithless, mindless approach-

Mr. Speaker, it is because of the great respect I have for the Speaker that I agree with you. I am delighted to learn that education is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, as if I ever had any doubt on that matter. However, I would remind you that the Bill which I was referencing, Bill C-96, which expresses the same kind of governmental mentality as Bill C-88, would cut about $5 billion from the education system of the country. That Bill originates in this Parliament rather than in provincial legislatures. Being the fairminded and objective person that you are, Mr. Speaker, you will acknowledge that fact. It is only because of the warped mentality that gives rise to a disinvestment in our youth through a cut in the education system that I make reference to Bill C-88 which indicates a lack of confidence in the Atlantic region.
Members ask how my comments are relevant to Bill C-88, which is merely a name change for CN Marine. Because you are a fairly objective, honest, caring, sensitive and dedicated servant of the House, you would obviously want to know how Bill C-88 represents much more than a simple name change of CN Marine. Members opposite laugh their way through this session and into oblivion. Oblivion will one day catch up with them for this insensitive behaviour.
Members should know that in Atlantic Canada the level of service provided by CN Marine, or the new company, Marine Atlantic Inc. as designated by this Bill, is not the pleasant scenic route by the sea. We in Newfoundland do not take CN Marine ferries for the pleasant scenic route by the sea. We take them because, contrary to popular opinion, we do not have trucks which float on water, and neither do we occupy, despite common misconceptions, God boots which allow us to walk on water. The CN Marine ferry service is the only way in which we can move our people, goods and services around the Atlantic region on a practical day-to-day basis.
This Bill does substantially more than simply changing the name of the service. It takes out of the pockets of CN Marine, the company which exists in advance of the passage of this Bill, some $30 million in accumulated revenues which the company has built up to allow it to fulfil its capital program which is to provide three new ferries for the East Coast ferry system. Through the new financial arrangements provided for in this Bill, $30 million is taken out of the pockets of CN Marine.
Those Members who sit amidst the glitter of the chandeliers, who are blinded by the shine of the marble, who are caught up in the richness of the texture of the wood and have forgotten from where they come may not think that $30 million is a lot of money. To the people of Atlantic Canada who are riding a ferry service little better than a cattle car, that $30 million represents an investment in the hope that the system might become civilized. This Bill takes that $30 million of accumulated revenue, hits it like a neutron bomb and vapourizes it away from the CN Marine company, in due course vapourizing the hopes of Atlantic Canadians to be served by a ferry service which indicates that the Government has some confidence and faith in and appreciation for the people of Atlantic Canada.
That is how my comments are relevant. I know that you, Mr. Speaker, feel much more informed and have much more empathy for the people of Atlantic Canada, having heard those pearly words of wisdom which I uttered on their behalf.
Before I was so rudely interrupted by Members opposite expressing their insensitivity for the region, I started to say that Bill C-88 was another step along the course of user-pay. Members should ask themselves what user-pay is. What is this concept which says that the people of Atlantic Canada shall pay a price to live in Atlantic Canada?

The result in the end will be the same. The Government of Canada, either because of insensitivity or, frankly, stupidity, will have altered the nature of the regions of this country by imposing a user-pay concept that strains and tears at the fabric of this country, which in turn defines for Canadians a sense of national identity and national unity. This Bill is an attempt to hive off the ferry services of Atlantic Canada which are essential in particular to the island province of my colleague from Egmont. They are essential to my own island Province of Newfoundland as a means of moving freight and people. The Government of Canada has lifted the gun to its shoulder, drawn the long bead with its eye, targeted the victim, Atlantic Canada, and this Bill is the bullet it intends to shoot into the heart of the economy of my region by attacking the most fundamental and necessary means of transportation in that region.
Members opposite may sit and huff and puff and twist and turn, but their silence is what Atlantic Canadians shall remember them for. They are only noticeable for and represented by the echo of their silence in this House, their inability to stand against the whip of party discipline and speak on behalf of the people who sent them here. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the adjournment debate tonight as a follow-up to the question I put on May 2 to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) concerning pensions for public servants, the military and the RCMP. It is now 10:03 p.m. and it has been a long day. I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that your day started about 15 hours ago, as did mine.
However, the day started many years ago for our federal pensioners, whether they were in the RCMP, the Armed Forces or the Public Service. I want to see that they get a fair
June 17, 1986

shake for their paid-for pensions. I feel that the Government is coming very close to making some type of an announcement on the pension issue. I hope to hear that good news before Parliament recesses for the summer. I wish to give credit to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and his staff who I know have been working for many months to ensure that an equitable solution is realized. They have certainly worked hard and long on this matter since we came to Government.
1 have asked questions in the House numerous times on this issue. The answers have been consistently the same; that is, the Government will keep the promises it made during the election campaign to maintain indexed pensions for those who paid for them. My role is to question the Government, when appropriate, and to defend the interests and concerns of my constituents in Ottawa-Carleton and, on occasion, those from other parts of Canada.
As Hon. Members know, in the National Capital Region, and in the riding of Ottawa-Carleton which I represent, there are many military people, many RCMP people and many public servants who are on pensions already. There are many more who will be on them very shortly. I feel it imperative to speak on their behalf, not to question policy directions which the Government might be taking but to question the issue of input into the decision-making process as far as their indexed pensions are concerned.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), referred to this same issue on June 12. In the Adjournment Debate he asked whether pensioners had been involved in the negotiations and, if so, at what level. He went on to say that he had asked numerous questions in the last year or so concerning the issue, as others and I have done in this Chamber.
The Public Service Alliance of Canada has been very effectively representing the concerns of public servants on their pension issues and those who will be receiving pensions shortly. The PSAC has been very vocal on their behalf at the bargaining table. The Federal Superannuates National Association has been doing all it can as well to represent superannuates. It has become slightly frustrated at the lack of full representation on the Minister's advisory council.
The FSNA has observer status on the council, but it does not have full membership. The council is composed of six members from management and six members from the union. The association would like to have more representation. The Minister has indicated that he is willing to expand the council to ensure that the association has direct participation. I suggest that there might be one elected person and one appointed person, which would give a stronger voice in an advisory capacity. I think that the RCMP should also have a representative on the council, either as an elected representative or as an appointed one. That representative could be a person who is on active duty in the RCMP or possibly one who has retired, again to give the RCMP a better voice in pension decisions.
Adjournment Debate
The Canadian Armed Forces Pension Association, represented by its duly elected President, Ed Halayko from London, and his colleagues, met with the President of the Treasury Board on February 5 of this year for the first time and had some input into the process. At that time, they expressed some of their concerns. As I am sure you can imagine, Mr. Speaker, these are very proud people. They are ex-servicemen and women and indeed we are very proud of the efforts they made to make Canada a safer place to live. I feel that they too should have more say and should have representation on the advisory council, possibly through an elected person or an appointed one. That would give them more input into decisions made on their pensions, but that has not happened yet either.
There is some confusion over responsibility for the management of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the RCMP Superannuation Act. The Canadian Armed Forces Pensioners Association, which speaks for about 75,000 retirees, though it has a very limited number of paid memberships, is concerned about the $13 billion it has put into the fund.
I would like to emphasize that it is important that a decision is made very shortly. I am disappointed that there was not more input into the process from retirees of the RCMP and the Armed Forces. I suspect we will hear very soon that the Government will keep its campaign promise to index pensions, and I hope that we will hear this before the end of the session so that we may take the good news back to our constituencies across the country. I hope we may be able to tell our constituents that a positive decision has been taken concerning pensions for all of those who paid for them and are very deserving of them.
Unfortunately, these people have not had as much input as they would have liked into the process, with the exception of PSAC through the bargaining table. However, in the months and years ahead, we hope the Government will see fit to include more of them on its advisory council so that the Government may listen to their good counsel and benefit from their many years of experience.

Mr. Speaker, I draw to the attention of the House the connection between government policies and human suffering in Africa, particularly in Ethiopia. Much of that suffering has been due to natural causes, but there is reason to believe that much of it has been due to the tragic excuse for leadership forced upon many of the countries concerned, especially Ethiopia.
For example, as was reported in the May 30, 1986 edition of The Globe and Mail, an assistant professor of economics at Bloomsburg University and a native of Ghana wrote that more than two million Africans perished from famine last year and that millions were still in danger. He continued by indicating that the basic causes of the agricultural decline in Africa could be found in Government policies of exploitation and oppression of peasant farmers.
To that I add the testimony of Dawit Wolde Giorgis, the defected head of Ethiopia's Relief and Rehabilitation Commission who is now in the United States, having turned his back on the Marxist Government of which he was once a part. He left it because of the contradiction he found between the support from the West which was needed by Ethiopia and the Soviet alliance to which his Government was committed. In an interview in The New York Times, he called it a drought problem but said that it was more of a policy problem. He went on to say that drought complicated the problem and that if there were no change in their policies, there would always be millions of hungry people in Ethiopia. Since then he has been interviewed by both the BBC and the CBC. In the course of those interviews he said:
The leadership in Ethiopia lives in a fantasy world created by its own policies and imagination.
It is evident that these policies of fantasy and imagination have contributed to the suffering of the people over which the regime presides through extravagant spending on military purposes. Almost half the national budget goes to the armed forces. Some $8 billion worth of Soviet military equipment is being imported by a country dependent upon the West to help feed its people and to help provide necesssary medical care.
To that we could add a tragic and indefensible human rights record of such magnitude that, according to the Economist's World Human Rights Guide, Ethiopia has the worst record of any country in the world. For example, there are an estimated 10,000 political prisoners at least. Some of them, like the family of the late Emperor, have been incarcerated for over 10 years without even a charge being brought against them. It is not only people of that standard. Only last week an Ethiopian man visited my office who had been released from a political prison in that country after being incarcerated for seven years simply on suspicion. He was allowed to go free finally when the police informed him that he was no longer suspect. He has never been charged, let alone found guilty of any offence against the country.
With that kind of Government in charge in Ethiopia, not only there but in similar Governments in charge in other countries of Africa, we have to be concerned as a Parliament with the way in which Canadian food aid, development aid, is being used. Is it being used to shore up radical, oppressive, militaristic regimes or can our Government use the leverage which is surely within its grasp to exert a moral influence on immoral regimes that can persuade them if not to turn to
June 17, 1986

justice, at least to moderate injustice? I am sure that great, great numbers of people in various African countries would cry out with gratitude to any democratic Government that would use the power within its grasp to act on behalf of those who cannot act for themselves. This is not to say we should not be as active in aid causes as we have been. Quite the opposite. But it is to say that we should not be active as an aiding and developing country without using the influence and the opportunities that are before us so that we can thereby lift the level of the lives of people for whom we have some responsibility and where we have some opportunity.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) has raised a critical issue. The Government of Canada clearly shares his concern over the possible diversion of necessary funds to accommodate needs within an individual country, particularly when the issue in the case of those who are drought stricken in Africa has been brought so well before us and is so well known to us, whether through press reports or through the specific efforts the Government has taken to determine for itself the needs and causes.
It would be unrealistic, however, for us from the Canadian Government's point of view to restrict our efforts in assisting those who are in dire need, dying of starvation and facing constant pressures, to that point where we were not assisting them where we could. We have made special efforts through special envoys and considerations to make sure that any aid we have provided finds its way to the necessary areas and to those people needing it. Those efforts are continuing.
It would be also unrealistic, in direct response to the question of the official who has resigned, to expect that with any Government, with any set of policies, with any bureaucracy, there would not be individuals or problems that would not compound certain situations. That could be said of any country anywhere in the world today. It would also be unfair to say that in this situation in Ethiopia or in other African countries similarly afflicted that policies themselves were the sole cause of the problem.
I could refer the hon. gentleman to the United Nations General Assembly debates several weeks ago, which Assembly was dealing with this issue. 1 am not sure if there was an emergency debate, but there was a full debate much in keeping with efforts made by other UN initiatives, such as the Bruntland Commission looking at environment and development. All of these issues overlap, and they are being considered.
Canada most of all from from public statements that have been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) is very cognizant of the special pressures that exist in Africa and has responded with special economic measures to try to help in a general way not only Ethiopia but other African countries to ensure that human rights are respected in so far as possible, whether in Africa or in other countries throughout the world.
Adjournment Debate
Our record is well established and we continue to try to improve it. We continue to try, where we can, to ameliorate and improve the condition of the people directly affected.

WOMEN-INQUIRY IF GROUPS SUBSIDIZED LAST YEAR WILL RECEIVE SAME AID THIS YEAR. (B) SIZE OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 30 I raised an extremely important question with regard to funding for women's organizations in Canada. The Minister replied, suggesting that the Department was not anticipating radical cuts but he would not be at all specific and certainly would not say that the women's organizations would not be getting adequate funding or even the same level of funding they received in the past. His reply covered up the fact that the Department itself does not seem to know how much money will go into the budget for women's programs. In fact, organizations have been given 40 per cent of the funding they received last year and they have no idea how much they will get for the full year. They are, therefore, not able to plan, and some organizations have experienced real difficulties.
The National Action Committee has reported that there have been delays for many organizations across the country. These have been reported to me and other members of our caucus by Quebec and British Columbia women's organizations which have had the same problem. The North Bay Women's Centre had to close down for four months due to delays in funding. The Regina Status of Women had its application turned down although they thought they had met the requirements. It took nearly a year to process the application of the Alberta Status of Women.
Media Watch has heard rumours that there will be cuts of between 5 per cent and 40 per cent. They have only been able to maintain their overhead and regular operations. They have had to put staff on lay-off notice twice this spring. A staff member had to leave because she could not live with the financial insecurity. The National Association of Women and the Law has had to lay off staff. On account of the Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association, the Parliamentary Task Force on Child Care has been extremely stretched and does not have funds to carry on the work it should be able to do.
The 1986-87 Estimates do not even list an amount for the women's department. There is only a global amount for something called citizenship development. That is a cut from previous years. We know that the 2 per cent cuts in discretionary spending will hurt the Secretary of State and women's programs especially because they are in a discretionary area.
Women's organizations have expected increases because they had been promised them in the past. There was a large increase in 1984, albeit perhaps for the wrong reasons. There was an election in 1984. The right thing was done, whether or not for crass reasons of political opportunism. Women's organizations were promised subsequent increases for the next five years and have not been getting them.

June 17, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Women's organizations play a vital role in Canadian society. They need and deserve stable funding. I do not think the Government understands that Canadian women's organizations are different from women's organizations in other countries. They are not the same as the organizations in the United States or Europe. They do extremely important work. They help to develop Canada. They unite urban and rural women, union and non-union women, women working full time in the home and women in the labour force, women from visible minorities, native women and disabled women. All kinds of women come together. This is a unifying force.
The women's movement has enormous support in Canada from women and men. It is a positive experience for people. It is social change which people see as beneficial. A few very small groups are trying to promote the idea that the women's movement somehow represents far-out groups which do not represent the vast mass of Canadian women. This is totally unsubstantiated. These groups are doing important work for Canada, which work is recognized by Canadians.
A better way to fund the work would be through the tax system. I would like to have a tax credit system instituted. In filling out their income tax forms and child tax credit forms, people would have the opportunity to allocate a certain amount of money to women's organizations. The same could be done for other voluntary organizations in culture, the environment and other areas which contribute to Canadian society. It is somewhat incongruous that the Canadian Government funds its own lobbyists. I think it would be far healthier if Canadian women and men could themselves decide which organizations to support.
In this kind of new way of allocating funds, the Government would be a bookkeeper on the basis of instructions in effect from taxpayers. I think that would be highly desirable. It could be a basis for stable funding and, of course, we want to see more funding for this extremely vital sector which does so very much for Canada. What we have instead, I am sorry to say, is a Government which does not give adequate recognition. We now have a crisis on our hands. In fact, it is only tomorrow that the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) will be meeting representatives from some 60 women's organizations. They are being flown to Ottawa to discuss a crisis which need never have occurred at a substantial cost, more than $70,000, which is more money than some organizations get in their regular funding.
To conclude, I call on the Government to see that we have a stable, adequate system of funding for women's organizations that do so much for Canada.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: WOMEN-INQUIRY IF GROUPS SUBSIDIZED LAST YEAR WILL RECEIVE SAME AID THIS YEAR. (B) SIZE OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) is anxious to know whether women's groups who received
funding under the women's program last year will receive the same support again this year.
Several factors must be considered by the Department of the Secretary of State in determining which groups will receive Government assistance, and for which objectives and at what levels.
A number of factors must be considered.

The existing track record of groups is important. To what extent have they fulfilled their objectives over the past year? What are their priorities for the coming year and how do these accord with the priorities of the women's program? The number of requests received in the various areas for which funding is provided is obviously another variable. Equally important is the amount of money available for grant purposes.

As Hon. Members are aware, all departments have been asked to help reduce the deficit by proceeding with certain budget cuts.

The Secretary of State was most anxious that the women's program of his Department not experience heavy cuts in view of the program's absolutely essential role in promoting the advancement of women. It is not only an essential role, it is a catalytic role, one which cannot be easily replicated.

The Minister is very broadly committed to ensuring that there will be no severe cutbacks in the women's program, and the result is there will be only a 5 per cent cut, which is certainly reasonable if we consider that reducing the deficit, like advancing the status of women, is one of the Government's priorities.
On June 26, the Secretary of State will be meeting with representatives of 58 women's groups to discuss ways of minimizing the effects of this cutback. Our Government's commitment to promoting the status of women is important. The women's program is an excellent vehicle for disseminating subjects of interest to women, promoting their autonomy and improving the economic conditions they have to face.

Now that the program's budget level is known, decisions will be going ahead on the many worthy applications received. I understand that last year the women's program funded over 700 organizations. The funding covered diverse issues such as violence toward women, economic independence, the Charter of Rights, legal, health, cultural and educational matters.

Mr. Speaker, as I said before, it is clear that the Secretary of State intends to continue his vigorous support of women's organizations in Canada.
June 17, 1986
